content: Tobacco use is the leading cause of preventable disease, disability, and death in the United States. Each year, nearly 480,000 Americans die prematurely due to smoking or exposure to secondhand smoke, and approximately 16 million people live with serious illnesses caused by smoking. Smoking damages multiple organs, including the heart, lungs, kidneys, stomach, and intestines, and is a major contributor to the development of various cancers. Quitting smoking significantly reduces health risks, including cardiovascular disease, stroke, and cancers of the mouth, throat, esophagus, and bladder. Within 10 years of cessation, the risk of lung cancer is reduced by half. Epidemiology Tobacco use accounts for over 480,000 deaths annually in the United States, representing one in every five deaths. Approximately 34.5 million adults in the U.S. currently smoke cigarettes. Alarmingly, every day, more than 3,800 youth under the age of 18 smoke their first cigarette. Smoking-related diseases cost the U.S. nearly $170 billion annually in medical care. Smoking and Health Death Due to Smoking Cigarette smoking is the leading preventable cause of death in the U.S., causing over 480,000 deaths annually. It increases the risk of death from all causes in both men and women. Smoking is responsible for 80% of deaths from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It also leads to diminished overall health, increased absenteeism from work, and higher healthcare costs. Smoking and Cardiovascular Disease Smoking causes stroke and coronary heart disease, two of the leading causes of death in the U.S. Even smoking fewer than five cigarettes a day can result in early signs of cardiovascular disease. Smoking damages blood vessels, causing them to thicken and narrow, which can lead to blockages. These blockages can reduce blood flow to the brain, resulting in stroke, or to the legs and skin, causing peripheral vascular disease. Smoking and Respiratory Disease Smoking damages the airways and alveoli in the lungs, leading to lung diseases such as COPD, which includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis. Smoking is the primary cause of lung cancer. For individuals with asthma, tobacco smoke can trigger or worsen attacks. Smokers are 12 to 13 times more likely to die from COPD than nonsmokers. Smoking and Cancer Smoking can cause cancer in nearly every part of the body, including the bladder, blood (acute myeloid leukemia), cervix, colon, rectum, esophagus, kidney, ureter, larynx, liver, oropharynx, pancreas, stomach, trachea, bronchus, and lung. Smoking also increases the risk of death from cancer and other diseases in cancer patients and survivors. If no one smoked, one in three cancer deaths in the U.S. would not occur. Smoking and Reproductive Health Smoking can impair fertility in both men and women. In women, it increases the risk of preterm delivery, stillbirth, low birth weight, sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), ectopic pregnancy, and orofacial clefts in infants. In men, smoking can reduce sperm quality, increasing the risk of birth defects and miscarriage. Other Health Effects Smoking weakens bones, particularly in postmenopausal women, increasing the risk of fractures. It also damages teeth and gums, leading to tooth loss. Smoking raises the risk of cataracts and age-related macular degeneration, both of which impair vision. Additionally, smoking is a cause of type 2 diabetes, with smokers having a 30–40% higher risk of developing the disease. Smoking also contributes to systemic inflammation, reduced immune function, and is a known cause of rheumatoid arthritis. Benefits of Smoking Cessation Quitting smoking reduces cardiovascular risks. Within one year of quitting, the risk of a heart attack drops significantly. Within 2–5 years, the risk of stroke decreases to that of a nonsmoker. After five years, the risks of cancers of the mouth, throat, esophagus, and bladder are halved. Ten years after quitting, the risk of lung cancer is reduced by half. Smoking Cessation Strategies General Principles The 5 A's framework is an evidence-based approach to smoking cessation in healthcare settings. It includes: 1. Ask about tobacco use. 2. Advise to quit. 3. Assess readiness to quit. 4. Assist in quitting. 5. Arrange follow-up care. Pharmacological Interventions First-line pharmacotherapy includes nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) in various forms (patch, nasal spray, lozenge, gum, inhaler), sustained-release bupropion hydrochloride, and varenicline. Second-line therapies, such as clonidine and nortriptyline, are also effective. Bupropion Hydrochloride: Dose: 150 mg once daily for 3 days, then 150 mg twice daily. Duration: 7–12 weeks, with maintenance therapy up to 6 months. Adverse effects: Insomnia and dry mouth. Initiate treatment 1–2 weeks before the quit date. Nicotine Gum: Dose: 2 mg for 1–24 cigarettes/day; 4 mg for ≥25 cigarettes/day (up to 24 pieces/day). Duration: Up to 12 weeks. Adverse effects: Mouth soreness and dyspepsia. Nicotine Inhaler: Dose: 6–16 cartridges/day. Duration: Up to 6 months. Adverse effects: Local irritation of the mouth and throat. Nicotine Lozenges: Dose: 2 mg if the first cigarette is >30 minutes after waking; 4 mg if ≤30 minutes after waking (4–20 lozenges/day). Duration: Up to 12 weeks. Adverse effects: Nausea and heartburn. Smoking cessation is a critical step in improving overall health and reducing the risk of numerous diseases. Effective strategies, both pharmacological and non-pharmacological, are available to support individuals in quitting smoking.
